chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, from Ibn Sinan, from Ibn Muskan, from Abi Basir, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said:
"There is no wudu (ablution) due to vomiting."

(29) 29 As for the hadith narrated by Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Bint Ilyas, who said: "I heard him say: I saw my father, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, after he had performed wudu, having a flowing nosebleed, so he performed wudu." It is possible that what was meant here by performing wudu was washing the place, because cleaning a limb is called wudu, since it is derived from al-wada'ah, which is beauty. Do you not see that if someone washes his hand, cleans it, and makes it fair, it is said: he made it clean; and it is said: so-and-so is bright-faced, and a people are fair-faced. The poet said: generous in deeds, possessed of deliberation, weighty, and their faces are radiant. Al-wadu' with fathah on the waw is the name of that by which wudu is performed, while al-wudu' with dammah on the waw is the verbal noun, and likewise al-tawaddu'. Similar to this is al-waqud with fathah on the waw, which is a noun for that by which fire is kindled, while al-wuqud with dammah is the verbal noun, and similarly al-tawaqqud. If it is said: how can you carry the report upon the implication of the wording of the language when in the Shari'ah and convention it has shifted to the specifically defined acts? Do you not see that if one says, 'I performed wudu,' nothing is understood from it in common usage except the wudu of the Shari'ah, and it is not said absolutely of one who washed his two hands or washed one limb of his limbs that he performed wudu. It is said in reply: the unrestricted expression, even if it has shifted in convention to what you have mentioned, its construct form has not shifted; rather, the construct takes its meaning according to that to which it is annexed. Do you not see that if one says, 'I performed wudu from hadath' or 'for salat (prayer),' nothing is understood from it except the specifically defined acts in the Shari'ah? But if instead he says, 'I performed wudu from food' or 'I performed wudu for food,' nothing is understood from it except washing the limb and cleaning. And what is in the report is that he said: 'I saw my father, after he had performed wudu, having a flowing nosebleed, so he performed wudu.' So its implied meaning was that he performed wudu from it. Had he stated explicitly and said, 'He performed wudu from the nosebleed,' nothing would have been understood from it except washing the limb, just as when one says, 'I performed wudu from food,' nothing is understood from it except cleaning the specific limb. And that which clarifies this interpretation...

key_terms.الشَّرِيعَةِ: the Shari'ah, where wudu refers to the specific ritual acts
key_terms.اللُّغَةِ: linguistic usage as distinct from technical legal usage
key_terms.الْقَيْءِ: vomiting, discussed here as not requiring ritual wudu (ablution)
key_terms.وُضُوءٌ: ritual wudu (ablution), or linguistically washing/cleaning depending on context

ai.seo_question: Does vomiting or a nosebleed invalidate wudu (ablution) in Shi'i hadith?
ai.summary: This passage states that vomiting does not require wudu (ablution). It then addresses a separate report about nosebleeding by explaining that the term wudu in that context can linguistically mean washing and cleaning the affected area rather than the ritual wudu of the Shari'ah.
